en: Having approached the one dwelling in the hermitage, seated at ease, learned in the Vedas and Shastras, and possessed of a restrained mind, the sages questioned Yama.
O great sage, tell us by which specific vows those sages who are joined with major sins (mahāpātaka) as well as minor sins (upapātaka) are purified. YSS 1.2.
Yama says:
Water touched by the sun and wind during the day, by the stars and wind at night, or by the two twilights, is always pure. (YSS 1.3)
Water that is naturally pure, never defiled by impurities, and whether contained in a vessel or resting on the ground, is purifying for human beings. (YSS 1.4)
But if a twice-born man is touched by impurity, whether by night or by day, he shall immediately bathe and touch fire; he is always pure during the two twilights.

If a man is bitten by wild beasts, camels, horses, and the like, or by humans—provided it is not during their habitual haunts—he becomes pure immediately after bathing; this applies even during the periods of twilight and at night. (YSS 1.5)
If one has eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance due to some cause,
one becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.

Those who have perished by water or fire, by hanging, or by falling; those who have died after renouncing the world or through fasting; those who have sought death by poison or by leaping from a precipice, and those who have been killed by the stroke of a weapon.
These nine, having fallen away and being excluded from all religious duties,
are purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or by two Taptakṛcchra penances.
Those wicked ones who dwell in both [realms] and have fallen from Śyāma and Śabala are purified by the two sons of Indu, provided they give a cow and likewise a bull.
Having cremated one killed by a cow or a Brahmin, or one who died by hanging,
or having cut the noose [of a suicide], one should perform the *sāṃtapana* *kṛcchra* penance.
If one is afflicted by worms born from a wound or attacked by flies and the like due to contact with delusion, one should perform a Parāka penance for one year as a difficult austerity.
The wise know that for each individual sin committed, there is an expiation;
however, when there is a confluence of all sins, no expiation exists.
When all sins have accumulated, the wearing of a skull is prescribed;
the wise declare that this Kāpālika practice is the foremost atonement for it.
For those who eat the food of Kāpālikas and likewise for those who have sexual intercourse with their women,
a year-long *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed if done intentionally, and two *aindava* penances if done unintentionally.
Whether one has consumed *surā* liquor or even eaten beef,
one is purified by the *mauñjī-homa* after being afflicted by the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
If the performer dies once the penance has been determined,
he becomes pure on that very day, both in this world and in the next.
As long as even one person who is not a separate entity undergoes the penance,
those who touch him— even if they are themselves unworthy— shall become censured.
They are not to be shared meals with, nor accepted as gifts, nor allowed to study together, nor to intermarry;
yet when their vow is completed, they are all purified and become entitled to inherit property.
A child who is less than sixteen years old, as well as one who is eighty years of age,
women, and the sick, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
For one who is less than sixteen years of age but more than four years old,
his brother, father, or another relative shall perform the penance.
Therefore, for this most ignorant one, there is neither offense nor sin;
he incurs no royal punishment, nor is any expiation required.
Having killed one born of a mixed caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance;
but having killed a *sūta*, a *kuṇḍa*, or a *golaka*, one must perform the *atikṛcchra*.
Having killed women without distinction, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
likewise for killing a cow, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra born of an Anuloma marriage.
Having eaten from these, having gone to their women, and likewise having accepted gifts from them,
one should properly perform either a year-long *kṛcchra* or a single *abdakṛcchra* for the sake of purification.

While causing the death of another living being, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and constantly perform the *kṛcchra* penance; specifically, the *prājāpatya*, such is the established rule. (YSS 1.24)
Even all four who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka) without distinction are purified by entering the fire or by bathing at the Horse Sacrifice (hayakratu).
But those who perform secret rites, by reciting the Puruṣa-sūkta and the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn while standing within the water during the month of Māgha, become purified. (YSS 1.26)
Having engaged in sexual intercourse with another's wife, a man, a eunuch, or even with horses, goats, sheep, or cattle,
one should mutter the Pāvamānī verses for three days.
Those who engage in sexual intercourse with women such as Caṇḍālas or with cows are purified by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn for a fortnight while observing a vow of subsisting on milk.
Having approached his mother, the wife of his guru, a sister, or likewise a daughter, he must enter the fire; no other purification is prescribed.
Having approached his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, his own daughter, his maternal uncle’s daughter,
or his son’s wife, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six months.
Having approached six on the father’s side and four on the mother’s side, as well as others,
and those of the same lineage (sagotra), one should perform the Parāka Kṛcchra penance.
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker,
the fisherman, the stage-player, and the wrestler are those who dwell at the very edge of society.
Having eaten or drunk from these, or having entered into their presence in secret even once,
or having engaged in sexual intercourse with them in the mouth, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
As well as Caṇḍālas and Muṣṭikas, and likewise those born of mixed unions.

Having eaten the food of these [outcastes], having had sexual intercourse with their women, and likewise having accepted gifts from them, a year-long *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed if done intentionally; if done unintentionally, it is recorded as an *aindava* (moon-observance).
Those women for whom the drinking of liquor is remembered as a family custom,
though born from a fallen field, are known as those who follow improper family conduct.
Those who, though outsiders among all four castes, consider themselves to be Brahmins,
are by lineage of mixed origin and must be avoided with great effort.

He who is born from a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇī woman who has fallen after being married, and he who is born from one of the same lineage (sagotra)—both of these are to be known as Caṇḍālas. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.36)
One born from an adulterer upon a woman of the same caste is called a *kuṇḍa* while the husband is alive;
if the husband is dead, he is named a *golaka*. Likewise, both of these are considered outcasts from their caste.
Those who are procreated by twice-born men upon women of a different caste,
and upon all the wives of others, are remembered in tradition as *kuṇḍas* and *golakas*.
Their maternal castes have not been declared by you, nor are their paternal castes recorded;
such sons are ineligible for marriage with kinsmen on either the father’s or the mother’s side.

Speech uttered by those dependent on their mothers, by those allied with the king, by children and the elderly, or by those oppressed by the king, is certainly not authoritative; for they have no reply and have not been trained. (YSS 1.39)

The slayer of a horse, the slayer of a human, the cutter of trees cultivated for domestic use, and those who are attached to another's wife—these are not exempt from punishment; they are to be executed by the sword.
One who, with a malicious intent, kills another— whether it be a wife, children, or spouse,
as well as fields, grain, wealth, or the body itself— should be executed by blows from falling mallets.

The perpetrator, the consenter, the instructor, the encourager, and the obstructer; the minister, the associate, the co-resident, the one who should not be killed, and the one whose innocence is doubted—these are the persons with whom a man must deal with caution. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.42)
If a person who is devoted to and dependent on a devotee commits an offense against him, the responsibility for that act rests with the offender;
however, when the food has been offered to the one who enjoys it, the giver of the food incurs no blame and is released from liability.
Others and yet others are struck by greed; thus, there are those who are both superior and inferior, as well as those who are merely others and merely inferior.

In a sacrifice, a marriage, or likewise at festivals—whether with those of equal status or those of unequal status—they say there is no fault in providing food if one engages in the preparation of cooked offerings for the sake of another year’s anniversary (parābdika). YSS 1.45.
Even one who provides weapons or gives poison and fire attains the highest state after a month if he has given for the sake of another,
provided that his engagement was for the purpose of accomplishing virtue, wealth, or pleasure, and not out of a desire to harm others.

Furthermore, if one who possesses an undiscriminating mind goes along taking either a vehicle or an elephant, those who know the law declare that there is no fault in that case; he is pure in that instance and likewise exempt from punishment.

Whether it be a wife, a daughter, a daughter-in-law born into the family, a brother, a son, a servant, or any other person, whoever is corrupted by a fault must be punished by the king; however, one who is not the perpetrator is not liable—this is the law of the lord.

Whether by the giving of material goods, by impartiality, by the performance of actions, or likewise by combat—he who abides in the mind of a man should be known as his companion in both happiness and suffering. (YSS 1.49)
Whether it be a large deer, a bird, a wild animal, or one of the same species, or even another [creature],
if a man kills it unprovoked— or a woman— the owner's cow must not be seized by him as compensation.
For indeed, whatever birth one may have among the classes of the twice-born, those who commit sins are not exempt from punishment for sacrifices and other rites;
yet serpents, when captured and bound during the offerings to the planets, do not harm others, being themselves unafraid.
Having caused that [debt] to be paid to the creditor by the king, the debtor should be released from his life and wealth by his own master.

For even when cattle and other animals die due to one's own negligence during discourses on the Dharma and its meaning, those who know the Dharma likewise declare that there is no fault there corresponding to the number of animals. (YSS 1.53)

If wild animals with fangs or cattle die while unburnt [in a forest fire], they say that the sin falls upon the one who set the fire to prevent the evil, and not upon the one who holds the rope in his hand. (YSS 1.54)
When one person is killed by many acting together, it is not known whose lethal blow caused the death;
therefore, having identified the killer among them through divine means, he must be turned back by those appointed by the king.
One who is free from sin may die at some point having already relinquished the life-force, as a result of the purification of their transgressions.
Having countered [opposing views] with reasoning and means of valid cognition, some say: "This is the proof;
the eternal inner self dies at some point," as sung by the Vedas and the questioned sages. (YSS 1.56)

For those who, desiring their own welfare, wish to perform purifying rites such as the Cāndrāyaṇa out of fear of sin—may they likewise obtain the fruit of association with the lamp of knowledge that dispels the blinding darkness. (YSS 1.57)
Listen now to the sequence of punishments and penances prescribed for those men who, having incurred the necessity of expiation, have failed to perform their vows. YSS 2.1.
But for one who, having himself confessed his sin, performs a vow of penance, no punishment should be imposed; for he has accepted both the vow and the penalty.
In the case of a minor offense (pātaka), there is no monetary fine; rather, there shall be corporal punishment for an equal fault.
In that case, one who fails to perform the prescribed penance (vrata) should be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas].
A young man who, having committed a minor offense (upapātaka), does not perform a vow, shall always first undergo a non-coercive penance for purification. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.294)
Having killed a blue jay, a frog, a cat, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, a Brahmin incurs [the guilt of killing] one hundred [of those creatures]; the same applies indeed for killing a mongoose.
One obtains thirty paṇas for peacocks, swans, and cranes, as well as for hawks, cocks, and likewise for wild peacocks.
A king should banish from his kingdom a Brahmin who has abandoned the sacred fire, neglected the twilight prayers, and performs service for a Śūdra.
But that brahmin who has relinquished the sacred fires, or who, even if he has not bathed or performed the mantras,
fails to worship and honor the sun at the two twilights— that twice-born one [is fallen].
One who does not perform the obligatory sacrifices, yet eats the food of a *vṛṣala*,
shall, even while living, pay a penalty every day with weapons.
Having confiscated all the property of a Brahmin who sheds semen upon Śūdra women or desires a Vṛṣalī, one shall brand the sign of the female organ upon his forehead.

Having seized all those who bear the mark of the Lord, the mark of wine, or the mark of liquor on their foreheads, as well as those who provide white garments to prostitutes, the king [shall punish them].

One who has performed an ablution for purification after death, one who bathes during the day, one who eats another's food even when it is his own, and one who neglects his religious duties— these are said by the King to be those whose wealth serves only their own selfish ends.

Having taken back everything that was given away by a Brahmin who has abandoned what was prescribed and resorts to the food of a Śūdra, one should present it every year to those who are learned in the Vedas.
If one uses an upper garment that is too small or too large, or commits an act of injustice, violence, or force,
or acts improperly toward a woman, he shall be made to pay double the fine.
Punishment is not ordained for children, the blind, the sick, or the elderly;
however, a man who voids urine on a road or similar public place incurs guilt.
Likewise, one should not discharge feces or vomit on the road;
he incurs a double fine if he should urinate while standing. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.16)
If one urinates while looking toward the direction of Indra (the east) or Varuṇa (the west), or likewise voids excrement there, one shall incur double the punishment. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.17)
A thief, a slanderer, an assailant, and the husband of a low-caste woman—
these five who have abandoned all restraint should be known as the thorns of the village.
Having banished these thorns from the realms after examining them, the king should do so;
for if they are not expelled, they bring darkness upon the world by practicing untruth.
One who is possessed by Viṣṭa and others, who is full and yet diminished, adorned with red garlands,
nourished by the work of a thief, and is himself a thief— such a person, when killed by the king, [brings about his own destruction].
Having placed the footprints of a dog and so forth upon his face and having covered him with a donkey skin,
one should place the slanderer upon a donkey and banish him after his wealth has been confiscated.
Having broken into houses, having stolen property, and having even made household utensils his own,
the king should banish from the realm the perpetrator of such violence, treating him as an outcaste.
Then, having combined two things— a broken vow and a vessel of liquor—
one should cast away the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, his heart smeared with ordure.
Furthermore, the king should cause one whose limbs are smeared with ashes, who is perfumed with the hair and bones of a corpse,
and who has abandoned the sacred fire, to be banished from the kingdom after confiscating all his property.
The king should cause a man who has transgressed the pledge to depart naked, fanned by human hair and with a crest bound upon his head with a garland of those same [hairs].
One should banish from the village that lowest of Brahmins, a son begotten by a Śūdra woman on a Kṣatriya father, who is a man whose very company causes sin.
But if one mixes a shedder of white semen with virtuous men and feeds him in the same row, he shall incur the first amercement.
Wealth given, as well as the path studied by the twice-born and others, all becomes fruitless through the talk of treacherous men. (YSS 2.28)
But one who gives a flaw to the property of the gods, of Brahmins, or to his own kin, is suspended; a Brahmin who has stolen all wealth incurs the dissolution of his body.
He who provides an opening for thieves is called a thief himself;
having stolen all his property, one should brand a dog's footprint upon his face.
At night, during the evening, a man may discern the progenitor by means of signs;
likewise, having identified through signs one who speaks of emptiness, he should banish him.
Having punished the liar in the debate, the king should prescribe twenty vows for those witnesses who conceal [the truth] among the wicked. (YSS 2.32)
The observer of the vow, while wandering for alms and having not yet offered oblations to the sacrificial fire,
may eat a single morsel at each mealtime provided he is not ill.
A man who fails to rise in greeting for his teacher, father, brother, father-in-law, or king shall be made to pay a fine of three *paṇas*.
But when one is seated upon this supreme, established seat, the Śūdra attains the state of the six-footed [bee] as he proceeds on his journey. (YSS 2.35)
If the weight or the measurement of a commodity is found to be either excessive or deficient, except in the case of speech,
one should consider that property to belong to the king.
If a merchant sells sesame oil mixed with [other substances] under the name of ghee,
or if he sells ghee mixed with oils, he shall be made to pay four times the value of the oil or ghee.
Marīca should be made fourfold with pieces of stone, salt with clay, and asafoetida with the exudations of trees; thus it should be administered. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.38)
Furthermore, if a seller mixes grain with chaff or stones,
he shall be made to pay the value of that [grain], and he must also return the mixed substance itself.
Having mixed [the substance] with either similar or dissimilar materials, the fine for men is declared to be fourfold; therefore, one should always act accordingly.
One who throws away the sweepings of a cremation ground, filth, a skull,
or even chaff upon the road of a village shall be made to pay five *paṇas*.
The householder who discharges the flow of leftover water incurs a double fine;
the one who releases it is also punished with a silver fine.
Having killed a *kakara* during the day, a Brahmin shall pay a fine of three *paṇas*;
having killed a hare, a tortoise, a monitor lizard, or a ram, he shall pay sixteen.
A Brahmin who engages in the sale of milk, dairy products, salt, oil, and lac incurs the middle amercement.
One who sells cakes, cooked food, meat, soma, bone, honey, or skin shall incur the middle amercement. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.45)

The supervisor of the gambling hall, by overseeing the game, incurs the same penalty as the gambler; and the one who enjoys the stakes also incurs the same penalty as the gambler. (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra 2.46)
If a Brahmin should carry off a child born of a Śūdra woman from him, he incurs a fine of one thousand [paṇas];
the firstborn shall be the offspring [of the Śūdra].
A Brahmin who eats cooked food belonging to the husband of a *vṛṣalī* incurs a fine of fourteen *paṇas*; that amount is doubled during his period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*).
Having eaten at a *śrāddha* feast in that house, one incurs a fine of that same amount;
moreover, one incurs the first *sāhasa* penalty, especially if it was done without a valid cause.
One who eats at the Anvaṣṭakā or the Aṣṭakā festival while being the husband of a *vṛṣalī* incurs fourteen *paṇas*; likewise, the one who eats [with him] incurs a monthly fine.
Even while following the sequence [of the *krama-pāṭha*] as taught by the eightfold instruction, one who first eats at the house of a *vṛṣala* incurs half of ninety-six [faults].
A Brahmin incurs sixteen [units of demerit] for consuming forbidden foods such as liquor;
for fish that cause injury, he incurs twice that amount, one hundred.
In this manner, the Soma-drinkers should assign double the penance for these offenses;
however, one who eats the flesh of donkeys, horses, pigs, and the like is considered fallen (patita).
A twice-born man who maintains his wife by means of wood, bone, horn,
or stone incurs a fine of one thousand [paṇas] if he undergoes the shaving of his head.
He who, on the limbs or exposed parts of the body, makes a wound with his fingernails upon his wife,
or causes another to do so, shall be made to pay the first fine with his own body.
A twice-born man who eats from the mouth of a woman, or drinks from her cup,
as well as one who causes her to eat from his own mouth, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
A Brahmin who excessively teaches [forbidden knowledge], or who approaches a woman as if she were a horse, or kisses her private parts, shall become fallen (patita). (Yājñavalkyasmṛti 2.57)
Having intentionally discharged semen, a Brahmin shall pay fifty;
but having engaged in sexual intercourse with cows, he shall likewise be made to pay one hundred.
Moving thus, one attains the birth of a goat;
by proceeding into the wombs of buffaloes, one incurs the middle amercement.
A man who approaches a cow in her season incurs a fine of one thousand;
likewise, for those practicing vows, these fines become doubled.

To one who is equally weary on the road, a traveler should give either a portion of the way or a resting place; for one who gives neither advice nor shelter becomes like a ram of Yama, the giver of death.
Indeed, by serving a Śūdra woman, a Brāhmaṇa is declared to have become inferior to a Śūdra;
merely by approaching a Śūdra woman, he becomes fallen.
By the mere act of approaching a Śūdra woman, a twice-born man becomes absorbed in that [status] through his offspring;
however, they declare that the mother of such a child incurs a fall from her caste.

Therefore, whether for the sake of a sacrifice or for domestic purposes, a twice-born man who takes [fire] from a Śūdra who sprinkles white [seeds] into black [soil] becomes a destroyer of the sacred fire and awaits his downfall.
But having seen a son born of a Śūdra woman, they fall into great calamity; or the Vaiśyas take away his wealth by force, unless he himself [protects it]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.65)
Even among those who are empty and impure, a twice-born man who approaches a Śūdra woman will see the very beautiful Ajadanta; the ancestors will examine him.
Therefore, at śrāddha ceremonies, a twice-born man must certainly feed the Brāhmaṇas while setting aside a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman and even a dog.
Food touched by the husband of a Śūdra woman, looked upon by him, or mixed with his food—all such food is unfit to be eaten; however, this prepared food [is different]. (YSS 2.68)
Even if he is an equal among the twice-born, one should take grain from those who are unworthy of the company and inauspicious;
likewise, the husband of a Śūdra woman may take grain from such ranks.
Gold touched by copper, and likewise silver touched by tin, can be purified by the wise; however, that which has been touched during a *śrāddha* rite is destroyed.
A Brahmin who has been touched by a Kṣatriya woman, or likewise by the wife of a Vaiśya, attains purification through specific means; however, one who has gone to a Śūdra woman does not.
But that king who is indifferent toward a village or toward the husband of a Śūdra woman—that king is unfit to receive gifts; he is excluded from his own interests within that very village.
Among all thorns, indeed, the one who employs force is the most formidable;
therefore, the king should ordain a punishment involving degradation for those who act with violence.
One who commits a minor act of violence but later becomes a perpetrator of grave violence— having reflected that "sin indeed arises [from this]," the king should punish him.
In this way, from among the five [types of] thorns, the king should uproot them;
thus his righteousness, wealth, longevity, fame, and kingdom shall increase.
Regarding thorns, it has been stated that the fourfold action which is prescribed by the first method is accomplished through the path.
Kula and the others are authorized for the hearing of disputes because of the traditional transmission;
this has been understood even by the learned Brāhmaṇa Koṇa through the treatises. (YSS 2.77)
